title: Is Health Canada's Medical Marijuana Fiasco A Time Bomb Ticking Under Canadian Prohibition?

Posted July 13, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: Last year Ontario epileptic Terry Parker won a major victory from which he has not greatly benefited.
See
Canadian Court Says Lack of Provision for Medical Marijuana Violates Fundamental Rights; Gives Parliament 12 Months to Fix Marijuana Prohibition -- Or There Will Be No Marijuana Laws in Canada.

The Ontario court gave the Canadian government a year to come up with a workable plan to allow patients to have access to medical marijuana, or there will be no laws against possession in Ontario, Canada’s most populous province.

The government did not appeal the ruling, so the government must satisfy the court that its plan complies with its ruling.

In the unanimous Ontario ruling the court said, " An administrative structure made up of unnecessary rules, which result in an additional risk to the health of the person, is manifestly unfair and does not conform to the principles of fundamental justice…. "

Prohibiting these patients access to marihuana does little to enhance these state interests. What is required is regulation of this drug, as with tranquilizers, morphine and other much more dangerous and addictive drugs, for which there is also no doubt a large illicit market. "

As noted below, prominent Canadian Attorney, and Canada NORML founder, John Conroy, says, " Health Canada seems to have added criteria to the existing regulations which is not what the court told them to do…. You don't need photo ID for morphine or Demerol or any other prescribed medicine. "

Notice how this flies in the face of the court’s comments against " An administrative structure made up of unnecessary rules, which result in an additional risk to the health of the person. " Also note that they say, " What is required is regulation of this drug, as with tranquilizers, morphine and other much more dangerous and addictive drugs… "

Instead, Health Canada has required far more regulation of medical cannabis than of morphine and tranquilizers, which the court explicitly said are " much more dangerous and addictive drugs. "

Health Canada has made such a mess of this and has shown so little understanding of anything having to do with cannabis, that it seems unlikely that they even know how to put together a workable medical cannabis program.

Obviously, there is no way to predict what the court will do or when, but it is quite clear that Health Canada’s rules do not come close to complying with their ruling.

It is quite possible that the outcome will be the voiding of marijuana possession laws in Ontario, which will throw the matter into the parliament, which has previously passed a resolution, not a law, that medical marijuana should be available to Canadian patients.

Then they would have to pass a law, not just send best wishes, or marijuana possession would be legal in Ontario and they would still have a medical marijuana problem to deal with. Quite a mess.

This would come at time when there is overwhelming support for medical marijuana nationally, and a very large majority for legalizing possession, while Canadians are evenly split on the legalization of sales. There is also a raging national debate on cannabis prohibition.

Moreover, there will be a challenge to all aspects of marijuana prohibition in the Canadian Supreme Court latter this year. This is the context in which the Parliament would have to pass medical marijuana laws, which would satisfy the Ontario courts.

Immediately below is Health Canada’s press release. This is a classic exercise in bureaucratic confusion.

The second item below is an outstanding bit of journalism from Hour Magazine, a Montreal weekly. It describes the cannabis communities’ reaction to the regs.)

From Health Canada:
July 4, 2001
News Release

Rock announces medical marijuana regulations and progress report on research and domestic supply

OTTAWA - Health Minister Allan Rock today announced that the Government of Canada's regulations governing possession and production of marijuana for medical purposes have been approved and will come into effect on July 30, 2001. Minister Rock also announced research funding and provided a progress report on efforts to establish a domestic supply of marijuana for medical purposes.

" Today's announcement is a landmark in our ongoing effort to give Canadians suffering from grave and debilitating illnesses access to marijuana for medical purposes, " said Minister Rock. " This compassionate measure will improve the quality of life of sick Canadians, particularly those who are terminally ill. "

The approved regulations, which reflect extensive consultation with stakeholders, contain two main components authorizations to possess marijuana and licences to produce marijuana. They are designed to address issues relating to transparency of the approved process and the need for a clearer definition of medical necessity. These issues stemmed from the decision of the Court of Appeal for Ontario in the case of Regina v. Parker, rendered on July 31, 2000.

Draft regulations were pre-published April 7, 2001 for stakeholder consultation. Stakeholder concerns addressed in the regulations announced today include:

  • The application process will be managed by the individual applicant instead of a medical practitioner - reducing the burden on physicians and empowering the patient;

  • Applicants for a designated person production licence will not be required to submit a document proving that no foreign drug conviction exists;

  • The formula to calculate the number of plants permitted under a licence to produce will be adjusted to reflect estimated indoor and outdoor growing yields and margins of error; and

  • Transitional provisions will be included that extend all current exemptions by six months - ensuring patients are afforded an ample opportunity to comply with the new regulations.

The criteria for application and authorization to possess marijuana are clear: symptoms associated with terminal illnesses with a prognosis of death within 12 months; symptoms associated with medical conditions listed in a schedule to the regulations; and symptoms associated with other medical conditions.

The regulations were published in Canada Gazette Part II today. They come into force July 30, 2001.

Minister Rock announced other measures related to the Government of Canada's marijuana for medical purposes initiative. They include:

Outreach initiative to physicians to share information and seek input on streamlining application forms and process;

  • Ongoing review process involving physicians, patients, law enforcement officers and other stakeholders to monitor the effectiveness and application of new regulations and provide advice on future measures related to the manufacture, distribution and sale of marijuana for medical purposes,

  • Funding of $840,000 to conduct research on the efficacy of smoked marijuana in the treatment of wasting syndrome in those living with HIV/AIDS by the Community Research Initiative of Toronto; and

  • Final licencing approval of Prairie Plant Systems Inc. (PPS) of Saskatoon and provision of seeds which allows them to begin growing a legal supply and a wide variety of marijuana to supply the Government of Canada's medical marijuana initiative.

" The measures announced today are a result of an extensive consultative process and a commitment to be flexible, " concluded Minister Rock. " This approach will continue to guide our efforts as we monitor the implementation of these regulations and futher develop the supply and distribution process this Fall. "

From HOUR Magazine
July 12, 2001
By Charlie McKenzie
Close, But No Blunt

The criteria for application and authorization to possess marijuana are clear: symptoms associated with terminal illnesses with a prognosis of death within 12 months; symptoms associated with medical conditions listed in a schedule to the regulations; and symptoms associated with other medical conditions.

See
The Dutch Start Making Whole Cannabis Available By Prescription. Radio Netherlands Describes How Coffee Shops Work. -- 2 Items

Changes to the marijuana laws were required after the Ontario Court of Appeal ruled them unconstitutional and gave the government a year to bring them into line with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. With a doctor's prescription, the terminally ill, or those suffering chronic conditions such as AIDS and multiple sclerosis, will now be allowed to possess and grow marijuana - in quantities determined by their physician - or designate someone to grow it for them.

To prevent police hassles, patients and designated growers will be issued photo ID cards from Health Canada.

Health Canada, however, provides no legal source for marijuana, unless patients agree to participate in government research programs, nor does it provide a source of seeds or cuttings to start a crop.

While official Ottawa pats itself on the back, long-time activists across the country are sceptical of the whole program.

Hilary Black, founding director of Vancouver's Compassion Club and " Earth Mother " to the Canadian medical marijuana movement, vehemently opposes the new regulations.
See
BC Medical Cannabis Greenhouse Busted while Compassion Clubs Consult with Canadian Health Minister Allan Rock
and links

" The pretence of requiring a doctor's recommendation is based on stigma, control and fear, " she said. " We need to be making health care decisions based on health concerns, not legal catches. "

Nor does she think much of photo ID cards. " They're terrible, " she said. " There's a huge privacy concern here. Health Canada's record of maintaining confidential lists is not all that good, " she adds, noting that last year they allowed a confidential list of medical marijuana applicants to fall into media hands.

The absence of a safe marijuana supply also concerns her, but she is more critical of contracted marijuana growers (read: Prairie Plant Systems of Saskatoon), for using confiscated seeds to start their government sanctioned and subsidised crop.
See
Health Canada Gives $5.7 Million Contract to Company With No Experience to Grow Mediocre Weed for Medical Marijuana Research

Health Canada initially hoped to acquire tested seeds from the United States, but when negotiations with U.S. authorities failed, they opted to use seeds seized during drug busts.
(MarijuanaNews note: This really is like trying to get condoms from the Vatican.)

" Police confiscate those as evidence, " said Ms Black. " Government has no right using them for other purposes. They're stealing from a persecuted community and allowing a subsidised private corporation to monopolise the production of medicinal cannabis using stolen seeds. "
(MarijuanaNews note: Marc Emery offered to give Health Canada the seeds. There will be a story soon about seeds for Health Canada that will further demonstrate the absurdity of their handling of this business.)

The practise is not only ethically and legally questionable, she points out, but potentially hazardous to medical marijuana users.

" Growing plants without knowledge of their genetic make-up, " she warns, " is like reaching into a medicine cabinet blindfolded. "
(MarijuanaNews note: The Vancouver Club has a variety of strains available.)

Sources in the cannabis community report that Health Canada representatives have recently been spotted in Ontario hemp stores and lurking about court rooms where medical marijuana court cases are being tried, gathering information.

" The Feds obviously are trying to administrate something they know little about, " claims Marijuana Party leader, Marc-Boris St-Maurice.

" Where does government get its info " " from the cannabis community, of course, but without giving us credit. "
(MarijuanaNews note: The government seems to avoid anyone who knows anything about cannabis.)

St-Maurice and fellow activist, Alex Nehon, presently await the outcome of their trial for trafficking in marijuana resulting from their volunteer work with the Montreal Compassion Club. He finds the new regulations " mind-blowing. "
See
Montreal Police Arrest Operators of City’s Compassion Club; Health Minister " wouldn't comment on the arrests. "

" The application process is still too long, too tedious, " he said. " Why not license compassion clubs that have the expertise, structure and staff to help patients? "

Nor is he thrilled with photo ID cards.

" Only if they're easy to counterfeit, " he jokes, " Then I'm all for them. "

Lower courts in both Ontario and Alberta have substantially weakened the marijuana laws in recent months, but the Supreme Court has yet to deal with the matter. Later this year the court has agreed to hear a triumvirate of cases which, if successful, could overturn Canada's marijuana laws permanently.
See
Extraordinary Editorial in Winnipeg Free Press Outlines " Findings of Fact " In Possession Case to Be Heard by Canadian Supreme Court.

Abbotsford, B.C. lawyer John Conroy, a founding member of NORML-Canada, represents two of the three cases heading for the Supreme Court.

" The sole reason for photo ID, " he muses over the phone, " seems to identify one class of marijuana user from another - the sanctioned and the illicit. You don't need photo ID for morphine or Demerol or any other prescribed medicine. "

" It's absurd, " he said. " Especially since marijuana is considered by most to be a herbal medicine, something that should be available over the counter. "

" Health Canada seems to have added criteria to the existing regulations which is not what the court told them to do, " he adds.

" Unfortunately, most medical marijuana users will still have to choose between liberty and life. "
(MarijuanaNews note: that is a reference to the court’s ruling that " forcing Parker to choose between his health and imprisonment violates his right to liberty and security of the person. " )

The new regulations completely snub the network of compassion clubs that have sprung up across the country. Troubling as that is, they vow that until the marijuana laws are eliminated, its business as usual.

" It is quite possible that our work may become more civil disobedient, " says Hilary Black, " but we rather concern ourselves with doing what's right. Until Health Canada can provide clean, quality medical marijuana to every person in need, compassion clubs
will be there to fill that need. "
(MarijuanaNews note: I am very proud to have Hilary as a friend.)
